`cross()` calls `fare_for()` only to reject an unpriced class, then appends only `day`, `kind`, and `note`; `refund()` similarly appends `back: true` but no
   amount.  Later, `takings_between()` calls `fare_for(book, line["kind"])`
   for every selected line.  Since `set_fare()` replaces the single value in
   `book["fares"][kind]`, changing horse from 4 to 6 makes every retained
   horse line, including a spring line, count as 6d.

Since `set_fare()` replaces the single value in `book["fares"][kind]`, changing horse from 4 to 6 makes every retained horse line, including a spring line, count as 6d. On this reading the missing contemporaneous amount is a defect: the program cannot preserve the payment or repayment that actually happened.

It keeps fare changes simple—one replacement value—and lets the clerk quote the same current table through `quote`. But it cannot say how much cash was actually taken, returned, or left in the box in a past period; no line contains that fact and the old fare is discarded.

Tell the board that this is the book working as built, but that it is not a
   takings ledger in the ordinary historical-cash sense.  The repository does
   not merely happen to recalculate: its names and docstrings consciously make
   the fare table current, make crossing lines non-monetary, and direct the
   report to price them at the rate "as it stands."  The new 6d spring result
   is therefore the intended current-value figure for spring's horse traffic.

   That reading is the better description of the present code than calling the
   result an accidental defect.
